relations.subject: eventing:timer
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - promoted; repurposed from its original DurabilityLevel-scope-sharing use to a timeout-value inheritance fact, same shape (the same configured value applies at two structurally distinct scopes)
relations.evidence: Timers follow the same timeout semantics as their Parent Functions. So, if an Eventing Function has an execution timeout of 60 seconds, each of the timers created from the Eventing Function inherits the same execution timeout value of 60 seconds.

relations.subject: eventing:timer
relations.evidence: The Eventing Storage (or Metadata) collection stores information about timers and its association with an Eventing Function's handler.

relations.evidence: Bindings for Bucket aliases to keyspaces can be reused in timers. Bucket aliases, created during the Eventing Function definition, can be accessed by the timer constructs in the handler code.

relations.subject: eventing:timer
relations.evidence: callback - This function is called when the timer fires. The callback function must be a top-level function that takes a single argument, the context (see below).

relations.subject: eventing:timer
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - promoted predicate, applied to a newly-minted object
relations.evidence: Timers get automatically sharded across Eventing nodes and therefore are elastically scalable. Triggering of timers at or after a specified time interval is guaranteed. However, triggering of timers may either be on the same node (where the timer was created), or on a different node. Relative ordering between two specific timers cannot be maintained.

relations.subject: eventing:timer
relations.object: 832 to 1856 bytes per active timer (832 bytes + sizeof(context), default context max 1024 bytes)
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - promoted; object is a literal
relations.evidence: Each active timer an additional amount of space between 832 and 1856 bytes (832 bytes + sizeof(context)) is needed. Where the context by default is not larger than 1024 bytes.

relations.subject: eventing:timer-sharding
relations.object: 7-second active-timer scan interval; average firing delay ~3-4 seconds; worst case up to 14 seconds
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - promoted; object is a literal
relations.evidence: Couchbase currently scans for active timers every 7 seconds this creates a maximum delay of 7 seconds + the time it takes too process timers ahead of the given timer on a given thread. Thus, in an Eventing system in a steady state you will typically experience an average timer firing delay of about 3-4 seconds after the scheduled time.

relations.evidence: When using timers, it is required that all nodes of the cluster are synchronized at computer startup, and periodically afterwards using a clock synchronization tool like NTP.

notable_absence.finding: As on the Capella twin, no access-control or edition content appears anywhere on this page. Separately: this batch's eventing-memory-quota.md documents the Eventing Service's per-worker memory quota mechanics in detail (garbage collection, live-object heap pressure) but never once mentions Timer context objects as a contributor to that memory pressure, even though this page states each active timer costs 832-1856 bytes and 'With an increase in the usage of timers, the Eventing Storage collection's space assignment must also be increased' - the two pages describe adjacent resource-sizing concerns (worker memory vs. Eventing Storage keyspace space) without ever cross-referencing each other.

cross_component_finding: This page states extremely precise implementation numbers (832-1856 bytes per active timer, a 7-second active-timer scan interval, a 3-4 second average firing delay, up to a 14-second worst case, 'two or three inserts and then two or three deletes' in KV per timer) that are verified byte-identical to the Capella twin (cloud/eventing/eventing-timers.md, same sentences at the same relative positions) - yet the twin's round-8 extraction record captured none of them as concepts or relations; its relations stop at sharesOptionSetWith/requiresSetting/cascadesLifecycleChangeTo/hasBindingType/hasHandler. This is the third page in this batch (after eventing-lifecycle.md and, by the same 'no version marker' mechanism, eventing-language-constructs.md) where the Capella extraction is measurably thinner than the shared underlying content supports, reinforcing that concept-count differences between the two trees for a byte-identical page reflect extraction-round completeness more often than actual product differences.
